label: Engaged Cartesian natural philosophy and the defense of autonomous reason
description: Sor Juana was deeply versed in early modern Cartesian natural philosophy, using the Cartesian emphasis on rational clarity to argue that the human intellect has no sex.
historicalContext: Written in New Spain during the late 17th century amid the arrival of early modern European scientific and philosophical treatises in the viceregal court.
dialecticalTension: Applies Cartesian rational agency against the gendered scholastic hierarchies of the colonial Catholic institution.

citations.author: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
citations.work: Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz
citations.quote: Women are quite capable of philosophical contemplation; God has endowed them with intellect equal to men.

citations.author: Octavio Paz
citations.work: Sor Juana: Or, the Traps of Faith
citations.sectionOrPage: Part IV (The World and the Convent)

label: Inspirited Chicana feminist intellectual rebellion and epistemic autonomy
description: Anzaldúa explicitly claimed Sor Juana as a primordial spiritual and intellectual ancestor of Mexican and Chicana women speaking truth against patriarchal and colonial orthodoxy.
historicalContext: Chicana feminist intellectual renaissance in the late 20th century recovering suppressed Mexican women philosophers.
dialecticalTension: Transposes Sor Juana's baroque epistemic resistance into 20th-century mestiza borderland theory and queer decolonial critique.
